decisions.context: Millions of documents arrive daily, and volume varies sharply by season. The brief sets no request-latency or freshness target.

alternatives.label: Scheduled batch prediction deployment
pros: Seasonal volume: score large queues in scheduled runs
Serving cost: write results for consumers to retrieve
cons: Freshness: results wait for the next run
Multiple consumers: requires shared result storage

alternatives.label: Online computation serving
cons: Seasonal volume: must handle peak request load
Serving cost: keeps prediction capacity available for requests

decisions.rationale: Seasonal volume and serving cost decide the choice: scheduled scoring handles large, variable workloads without requiring an online response path. This gives up immediate predictions; the design point is novel and unattested, and sources including “Architecting a Machine Learning Pipeline” and “Three Levels of ML Software” describe batch deployment patterns.
consequences: Consumers retrieve completed results from shared storage.
Classification freshness depends on the scoring schedule.

decisions.context: Classification volume changes substantially across the year, so fixed capacity risks either peak overload or idle resources. The brief does not specify infrastructure or budget limits.

alternatives.label: Elastic resource scaling
pros: Seasonal volume: capacity follows workload demand
cons: Throughput: scaling may lag sudden bursts
Serving cost: added scaling controls and capacity planning

alternatives.label: Replicated mutable model instances
pros: Throughput: replicas can serve work concurrently
Seasonal volume: capacity can be increased by adding instances
cons: Serving cost: replicas consume capacity while running
Operations: mixed evidence and mutable replicas add coordination

decisions.rationale: Seasonal volume decides the choice: elastic capacity can track demand, with cost control as a secondary benefit. This gives up the predictability of a fixed replica pool; “Architecting a Machine Learning Pipeline” and “Productionizing Machine Learning with a Microservices Architecture” support demand-scaled resources.
consequences: Capacity limits and scaling behavior need operational tuning.
Peak workloads may still queue while capacity grows.
The checked design point is novel and unattested.

decisions.context: Operators need to see when classification quality drifts. The design space treats monitoring practices as combinable, and the brief does not say when labels become available.

alternatives.label: Input and feature-drift monitoring
pros: Drift visibility: detects changes in inputs and feature distributions
Operator response: can surface shifts before labels arrive
cons: Quality visibility: drift does not prove classification errors
Operator response: thresholds and follow-up need configuration

alternatives.label: Real-time prediction-quality monitoring
pros: Quality visibility: measures model behavior and prediction quality
Operator response: gives direct evidence of degradation
cons: Drift visibility: does not by itself explain input changes
Quality visibility: depends on ground-truth labels being available

alternatives.label: Periodic model health checks
pros: Quality visibility: can assess model health over time
cons: Drift visibility: changes may go unnoticed between checks
Quality visibility: slower signal than continuous measurement

decisions.rationale: Drift visibility decides the initial choice because the brief explicitly requires operators to see quality drift, and input shifts can be monitored without assuming immediate labels. This gives up direct confirmation of prediction quality; “MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning” and “Machine Learning Monitoring: What It Is, and What We Are Missing” describe drift monitoring. Pair it with quality monitoring once label availability is established.
consequences: Monitor input and feature distributions over time.
Define alert thresholds and operator follow-up.
Add label-based quality measurement when labels are available.

uncovered: Prediction freshness or response-time target and batch scoring cadence.
How results are exposed to several consuming teams, including interface and access controls.
LLM provider, model selection, prompt and model versioning, and fallback behavior.
Document retention, privacy, security, and audit requirements.
Label availability and delay, drift thresholds, and retraining or remediation policy.
Seasonal peak rates, cost ceiling, and deployment infrastructure.
